The combination of a concentration of investments in AI and rising government debt will now face a completely different level of interest rates than in the past. Here, there are clear risks of setbacks, and if risk

13 appetite declines, it could lead to us also needing to adjust monetary policy in a more expansionary direction. But this is not what our forecast and our policy rate path reflect, instead it is based on strong economic activity and elevated inflationary pressures that motivate an initial increase in the policy rate during this year. Overall, I think that it is reasonable to wait and not change the policy rate today but at the same time to clearly communicate that it is likely that the policy rate will be increased before the end of the year. The current policy rate is in my opinion somewhat expansionary and has contributed to supporting the recovery in the Swedish economy. The policy rate path in the draft report also reflects what I think is a reasonable assessment of how monetary policy should be tightened going forward. But as I mentioned initially, the exact amount that the policy rate needs to be raised is something we will have to test our way forward. When we began to cut the policy rate in 2024, after the high-inflation period, we often emphasised the importance of taking a learning approach.5 And I believe that this is a good starting point also now that we are moving towards raising the policy rate in an uncertain environment. Deputy Governor Per Jansson At the monetary policy meetings in June and August, I discussed the inflation picture in Sweden, concentrating primarily on three factors. These were: the prevailing inflation rate at the outset; the strength of demand-driven inflation; and the inflationary effects associated with supply shocks in the global economy, with a primary focus on the war in the Middle East. I still regard these factors as crucial to our inflation picture and therefore intend to update my views on

them in my comments today. As regards inflation at the outset, we have received one new inflation outcome since our last meeting, for August. Having been higher than expected in both June and July, inflation in August was broadly in line with our latest quantitative forecast from the Monetary Policy Report in June. In terms of the CPIF, inflation was 0.7 per cent and in terms of the CPIF excluding energy prices, it was 0.5 per cent. In essence, the outcomes showed a sideways development for both measures compared with the July figures. It was particularly pleasing that price rises excluding energy prices, which had surprised significantly on the upside in July, were entirely in line with our June forecast in August. Adjusted for the direct effects of the temporary fiscal policy measures, which we try to see through in monetary policy, the corresponding figures for inflation including and excluding 5 See, for instance, my speech: Aino Bunge: Inflation is in the process of stabilising at the target, but the way forward is not entirely smooth | Sveriges Riksbank.

14 energy prices were 2.2 and 1.6 per cent. These, too, imply a sideways development compared with July. At the same time, measures of short-term price changes – to which I attach quite considerable importance in my monetary policy considerations – have not continued to rise as alarmingly rapidly as they did earlier in the summer. As regards the key inflation measure which excludes energy prices and temporary fiscal policy measures the outcome at an annualised rate for the last six months does still remain some way above 2 per cent, and there are as yet no signs of a downward turn in this measure. However, the upturn since July is small, and when calculated over the last three months, the corresponding price increases have fallen significantly, from nearly 4.5 per cent to just over 3 per cent. This is of course positive. It is still primarily travel-related services that play a major role in the development of the inflation measures at higher frequencies. One explanation is probably the high level of tourism in Sweden this summer. It may also have been combined with so-called dynamic pricing, where companies use new technology to quickly adjust prices in line with demand. If this is what has driven up the prices of many travel-related services, there is every reason to believe that the upturn is temporary and that prices will fall back in the autumn as demand from tourism declines. However, the price rises may also be due to unexpectedly large indirect effects of the supply disruptions, such as more expensive jet fuel. The conflict in the Middle East shows no signs of abating – quite the opposite, in fact. Consequently, prices for energy components have continued to rise since our August meeting. I’ll come back to this development in a moment.

If this is largely the reason behind the higher prices for travel-related services, the price rises may well remain at an elevated level during the autumn. With that, I move on to the second factor: the strength of demand-driven inflation. At our meeting in August, I concluded that we did not yet need to worry about the Swedish economy overheating, but that the risk of a slightly faster demand-driven inflation had increased. The conclusion was based on several indicators showing that the economic upturn was on firmer ground. Since the August meeting, Statistics Sweden has published National Accounts for the second quarter, and they confirm that GDP growth has been both strong and broad-based. The outcome was even higher than Statistics Sweden’s already strong early monthly statistics. Seasonally adjusted quarterly growth came in at 1.6 per cent, compared with 1.4 per cent in the monthly statistics.

15 Admittedly, it cannot be ruled out that the rapid growth was partly due to one- offs. However, the upturn was broad-based – all expenditure components of GDP, apart from inventory investment, contributed to it. Furthermore, the Economic Tendency Survey, Purchasing Managers’ Indices and the Riksbank’s Business Survey all show indicators on healthy and improved levels. This makes me feel relatively optimistic about the conditions for growth in the Swedish economy going forward. As I mentioned in August, part of the picture is that fiscal policy is unusually expansionary. There is a risk of it becoming even more expansionary in the light of election pledges with unclear funding. It is also worth noting that activity in the labour market has now gradually begun to pick up. My conclusion from this reasoning about economic developments is that the risk of a demand-driven rise in inflation has increased further since August. One relevant circumstance in this context is that this is happening at the same time as conditions on the supply side of the economy are deteriorating. As I have mentioned previously, prices for several energy components have continued to rise since August, including crude oil, gas, petrol, diesel and jet fuel. Electricity prices – which are of considerable importance in Sweden – have fluctuated sharply and, overall, also shown a slight upward trend. This price development is largely due to the path to peace in the Middle East having become increasingly distant. Instead, the conflict has escalated, with more parties involved and a wider geographical dispersion. Alongside the war in the Middle East, other significant supply disruptions – related to, among other things, US trade and foreign policy, Russia’s war in Ukraine and extreme weather – are doing little to alleviate concerns about the supply side of the economy. From an

inflationary perspective, the combination of rising demand and supply- side constraints and shortages is a dangerous phenomenon. We all remember how inflation rose more or less unchecked in 2022, when a very rapid surge in demand following the pandemic coincided with rising costs for businesses in connection with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The situation was unique in many respects, and it is unlikely that it will be repeated in exactly the same way. But today there are similar elements that require vigilance. Although the inflation levels seen in 2022 were exceptional, developments at that time underline how quickly inflation can rise sharply in an adverse scenario. Let me summarise my conclusions from this review for the inflation picture and monetary policy. As regards inflation at the outset, I see no major shifts – either in a better or a worse direction – since our meeting in August. It is, of course, positive that the forecasting error which arose in June and July largely disappeared in August. However, the picture regarding price rises over a shorter time horizon than the usual twelve months is broadly the same as before, with

16 somewhat elevated price rises for the key inflation measures that exclude the direct effects of the temporary fiscal policy measures. Overall, however, I still assess the initial position as mainly favourable. What has clearly deteriorated since August, however, is the inflation risk arising from the interaction between demand and supply. One factor that, in this context, makes this development a little extra worrying in Sweden is that the ongoing conflict in the Middle East is obviously not favourable for the krona exchange rate. In fact, it has been depreciating more or less continuously since the outbreak of the war. Against the euro, we are now just some per cent away from reversing the entire appreciation from 2025. Against the US dollar, the krona is still considerably stronger than at the beginning of last year, but there is a clear and persistent trend towards depreciation here too. Since shortly after the announcement of the August monetary policy decision alone, the krona has depreciated by around 2 per cent against the euro and by slightly more than 4 per cent against the US dollar. Against this backdrop, I support the decision to now revise up our policy-rate forecast relatively significantly, in line with the proposal set out in the draft Monetary Policy Report. The upward revision to the policy-rate path is greatest in the second half of 2027, when the policy rate is now expected to be just under 0.5 percentage points higher than in the June forecast. The reason I am not advocating an interest-rate increase at today’s meeting is that inflation at the outset remains relatively moderate overall. In a world of considerable uncertainty, it is prudent to make full use of the scope this provides to wait before taking further monetary policy action. I therefore also support the

proposal for a decision in the draft report to leave the policy rate unchanged at 1.75 per cent, as well as the forecasts and analyses presented in the draft. I would like to conclude by briefly commenting on my view of the policy-rate rises that I now support, in light of the critical stance I have previously expressed regarding insurance hikes in the policy rate. My scepticism about insurance hikes does not, of course, mean that I believe we should disregard the forecasts for inflation altogether and focus solely on actual inflation outcomes, waiting until these outcomes have risen to very high levels before taking action. Rather, the point is that we need to have sufficient confidence that the forecasts will prove broadly accurate. There is clear evidence in the data that economic activity is continuing to strengthen while supply-side conditions are deteriorating. The same applies to the continued depreciation of the Swedish krona and, indeed, to the concerns that the interaction between demand and supply could generate particularly strong inflationary pressures.

17 So I do not believe that the interest-rate rises which I now consider necessary stem from a more or less vague argument about the need for some kind of insurance. For some time now – ever since last summer – the policy-rate forecast has shown a slightly upward trend, as a result of the expected normalisation of the policy rate in an economic upturn. The forecast is now being revised somewhat higher, as the economic recovery has become more stable and stronger, and there are, in addition, several clearly identifiable upside risks surrounding the future development of inflation. The revision to the forecast is not insignificant, but nor is it dramatically large. Essentially, it still reflects a normalisation of the policy rate in an economy that is gradually improving. Deputy Governor Anna Seim I support the proposal to leave the policy rate unchanged at 1.75 per cent. I also support the forecasts and the deliberations in the draft Monetary Policy Report. I have learnt that in military contexts people often speak of the importance of situation awareness – the need to establish a common view of the situation before deciding what actions to take. This also seems to be a sensible starting point for monetary policy decision-making, particularly when the state of the economy is difficult to assess. Let me therefore begin by conveying my view of the economic situation. Media reports still give the impression that inflation in Sweden is very low. In August, measured inflation in terms of our target variable, the CPIF, was 0.7 per cent. But we need to recognise that it is artificially low because of the direct effects of the temporary fiscal measures, particularly the halving of the VAT on food, the reduction in fuel tax and subsidies for local public transport. Excluding

these, CPIF inflation is 2.2 per cent. Looking instead at the more underlying inflation excluding volatile energy prices, it was 1.6 per cent in August. Inflationary pressures are also stronger than normal (see Figure 22 in the draft report), with strong momentum (see Figure 21 in the draft report).6 As regards the risk outlook, I continue to see a risk of inflation being higher than in our forecast. Globally, a resolution of the conflict in the Middle East appears to be a long way off. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely restricted, Saudi Arabia has closed an important east-west oil pipeline, and the situation is highly volatile around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait by the Red Sea – another chokepoint for world trade. The highly charged conflict in the Middle East has now lasted for more than six months, and oil prices have fluctuated sharply and risen significantly since our monetary policy meeting in August. 6 Measures of shorter-term inflation have, however, fallen back somewhat since July, when they were fuelled by unusually rapid price increases in travel-related services.

18 Swedish food prices have risen at a moderate pace since the VAT on food was halved in April, and the first report by the Food Price Commission, presented in early September, suggests that the VAT cut led to a 5.5 per cent decline in food prices and was fully passed on to consumers.7 The underlying price increases that I expressed concern about last autumn therefore did not materialise. This issue has received considerable attention in the public debate, and my impression is that food companies have made an effort to pass on the VAT reduction and deliver lower prices. Over time, however, I see a significant risk of higher food prices in the wake of the supply disruptions and cost increases of the past year. As regards inflationary pressures, forward-looking indicators are particularly important, and I note that Swedish companies’ price plans are elevated. Figure 23 in the draft report, which presents a broad range of inflation indicators, supports the view that inflation is currently artificially low as a result of the direct effects of the temporary fiscal measures. Over the ten years covered by the figure, actual outcomes for the CPIF excluding energy have mostly been within the shaded area spanned by the various indicators. In recent months, however, inflation outcomes have been significantly below even the lowest values of these indicators. When inflation accelerated in 2022–2023, the figure shows that the mass below the blue line disappeared, and a similar tendency can be seen for the summer months of this year. Weak global supply conditions, and the risks surrounding them, are now interacting with stronger domestic demand in Sweden. GDP grew more than expected in the second quarter, and there are also signs that the labour market is now improving, which is of course a very positive

development. The economic upturn appears to be broad-based, as respondents to our Business Survey also attest. As I have said before, I consider the current level of the policy rate to be expansionary. If the neutral rate has risen, or is set to rise going forward, as a result of factors such as substantial investment in AI and government consumption, the current monetary policy may be even more stimulative. GDP growing faster than in our forecasts is consistent with that view, although expansionary fiscal policy has also strengthened household purchasing power and contributed to recent developments. Since inflationary pressures are higher than normal and the economy is now approaching normal resource utilisation, I consider it appropriate to adjust monetary policy in a tighter direction, in line with the policy rate forecast we present in the draft report. Given the major shifts in monetary policy over the past fifteen years – with a policy rate that was first 0 or negative from autumn 2014 to spring 2022, then raised by 4 percentage points over the course of a year 7 See https://www.regeringen.se/pressmeddelanden/2026/09/livsmedelspriserna-sjonk-med-55-procent- efter-halveringen-av-matmomsen/

19 and a half to combat the high inflation in 2022–2023 – it is understandable if the adjustments we now see before us raise concerns. But I want to emphasise that the hikes indicated by the policy rate path, if the outlook for inflation and economic activity holds, are part of a normal economic cycle. The policy rate forecast is always highly uncertain. My assessment, however, is that, provided conditions do not deteriorate, this would be a gradual adjustment towards somewhat tighter monetary policy, cooling the economy slightly over a one- to two-year horizon so that inflation and resource utilisation stabilise. Given that I believe the policy rate should be raised – and have previously argued that an early increase could reduce the risk of more forceful tightening later – why am I not advocating an increase today? I have wrestled with this question, and today’s decision was not an easy one. But after several years of a prolonged economic downturn and persistently high unemployment, I have preferred to give the economy the benefit of the doubt and have seen a strong need to wait for reliable signals. The recovery appears robust, but the economy is supported to some extent by subsidies that make it difficult to gauge the strength of demand pressures. My overall assessment, nevertheless, is that we are now approaching normal resource utilisation, warranting somewhat tighter monetary policy to achieve inflation at the target over time and a real economy in balance. Unless something happens to overturn my current view of the economic outlook, I will therefore advocate a first policy rate increase at our meeting in November. But it is pertinent to once again point out that the policy rate path is a forecast, not a promise. As always, we stand ready to adjust monetary policy

And if futures prices continue to be wrong, so that

21 high prices on oil-related products persist, the risk of rising inflationary pressures increases. Given that the conflict between the United States and Iran is ongoing, we must take into account in our calculations that global market prices for energy and several commodities may remain high well into next year. It is quite possible that demand in the Swedish economy will continue to grow rapidly and faster than in our forecast. Then, at some point next year, we may see signs that capacity constraints are starting to bind in some sectors. If companies’ costs are simultaneously pushed up by persistent effects of supply shocks, companies may pass on the cost increases to prices charged to customers. The overall result can be that inflation is persistently pushed up to well above 2 per cent. In addition, there is risk linked to the weakening of the krona exchange rate that has occurred this year. Our inflation forecast is based on the assumption that the weakening is temporary and that the KIX-weighted exchange rate will strengthen again starting the first quarter of next year. If the krona were instead to continue weakening, the risk of higher inflation in the coming years would of course increase. The two most recent outcomes in Statistics Sweden’s Labour Force Survey have been strong in the sense that both employment and the labour supply have increased. As the supply has stayed apace with employment, however, unemployment has remained high. The forecast in the draft report entails employment going forward growing somewhat faster than the labour force and unemployment therefore falling, which I think is probable. There is of course uncertainty

over how long it will take before unemployment begins to decline more significantly. But, as I have said, the growth outlook is favourable, and hiring will probably increase as the economy strengthens further. Another risk factor that needs to be closely monitored is the rapid upturn we have seen in yields on bonds with long maturities. Rising long-term interest rates can, via various channels, have a negative impact on the outlook for economic activity and inflation around the world. These developments may have a negative effect on asset prices, increase the costs of loans with longer fixed-interest periods and worsen government finances in many countries that are highly indebted, such as the United States, the United Kingdom and France. Countries with low government debt are less vulnerable. From a Swedish perspective, this development underlines the importance of maintaining the fiscal policy framework in future government budgets.

22 Let me conclude by explaining how I have weighed the risks I have discussed here. The outlook for economic activity in Sweden is continuing to strengthen; the current proposed forecast entails resource utilisation, measured in terms of the GDP gap, normalising much earlier than we thought in June. This means that the need to support the recovery, which was the motive for cutting the policy rate from 2.25 to 1.75 per cent last year, no longer exists. At the same time, the supply shocks that were previously pushing up global cost pressures still remain, and once again the earlier futures prices for crude oil, for instance, have proved to be too optimistic. These circumstances, combined with a weak krona, indicate that the risks that inflation will be higher than the target of 2 per cent have increased. There are thus strong reasons to raise the policy rate to 2 per cent in the near term and also to revise up the forecast for the policy rate. My assessment today is that it is reasonable to raise the policy rate as early as in November. The forecast for the policy rate next year, which indicates further increases, is also reasonable yet associated with considerable uncertainty. For now, we can still sail in full sail, but in November we probably need to reduce the sail area. The speed will probably remain the same; Swedish growth is broad and solid.
